def: Application-Specific Integrated Circuit: a chip designed for one job and frozen at manufacturing. Best performance per watt, longest and costliest to develop.
Field-Programmable Gate Array: a chip whose logic can be reconfigured after manufacturing. Flexible, used for prototyping and moderate volumes; the industrial partner's HEVC products used one.
Register-Transfer Level design, written here in VHDL: a textual description of registers, wires and logic that all operate in parallel at every clock edge.
Mapping RTL onto the standard cells of a given process (here TSMC 28 nm with Synopsys Design Compiler) to obtain area, timing and power figures.
Three ways of reporting silicon area after synthesis: number of equivalent gates, Design Compiler cell-area units, or square micrometres. Compare only like with like.
How many samples or pixels a module must absorb per clock tick to keep up with a resolution and frame rate at a given clock frequency.
The number of clock cycles between a block entering a module and its result coming out. A fixed latency for all block sizes lets modules chain without stalls.
Splitting a computation into stages separated by registers so that a new input enters every cycle while earlier inputs advance; delay lines of registers equalise the latency of parallel paths.
Performing a 2-D transform with a single 1-D core used twice (rows, then columns) and a transpose memory in between.
Read-only memory holds fixed data such as transform kernels or fixed ALF filters; random-access memory holds pixels and intermediate results. Both are counted in kilobits.
A true hardware multiplier that can multiply by any coefficient read from a ROM; sharable across transform types and sizes.
A multiplication by a fixed constant implemented as shifts and additions; cheap for one kernel, costly when many types and sizes are needed.
Splitting an N-point DCT-2 into an even part (the N/2-point DCT-2) and an odd part, recursively; it nests all sizes and halves the multiplications.
In VVC, the high-frequency half of 64-point DCT-2 and 32-point DST-7/DCT-8 coefficients is defined as zero, so large transforms process only a quarter of the block.
Multiple Transform Selection: VVC's choice of DCT-2, DST-7 or DCT-8 for the horizontal and vertical primary transforms of luma blocks.
Low-Frequency Non-Separable Transform: a secondary matrix transform applied on the low-frequency corner of DCT-2 blocks; 4 sets × 2 kernels.
Members of the discrete trigonometric transform family used by VVC; DCT-8 is DST-7 with reversed input order and sign changes.
Adaptive Loop Filter: the last VVC in-loop filter, a Wiener-type diamond filter (7×7 luma, 5×5 chroma) whose coefficients are chosen by the encoder.
Cross-Component ALF: a 3×4 filter that refines each chroma sample from its co-located luma samples.
Adaptation Parameter Set: a bitstream structure carrying ALF coefficients and clipping values (up to 25 luma sets and 8 chroma sets).
ALF sorts each 4×4 luma block into one of 25 classes from gradient sums (directionality and activity) and applies a geometric transform (rotation, flips) to the kernel.
A line 4 luma (2 chroma) samples above each horizontal CTU boundary; ALF pads across it to avoid storing whole CTU rows in line buffers.
Memory holding a few rows of pixels across the full picture width so that a filter can see the samples above the block being processed.
Coding Tree Unit (up to 128×128 in VVC) and its per-component Coding Tree Blocks; split into Coding Units and Transform Units.
Chroma sub-sampling formats: 4:2:0 keeps a quarter of the colour samples, 4:2:2 half (professional video). They change throughput and memory requirements.
The brightness component (Y) and the two colour-difference components (Cb, Cr) of a video sample.
Filters applied inside the coding loop, identically in encoder and decoder: LMCS, deblocking, SAO and ALF in VVC.
Sample Adaptive Offset (per-category offsets against ringing) and the deblocking filter (smoothing of block edges), both preceding ALF.
Rate–distortion optimisation chooses the option minimising J = D + λR, where D is distortion, R the bit rate and λ the Lagrange weight.
Bjøntegaard delta rate: the average bit-rate difference (%) between two codecs at equal quality, computed over several rate points.
JVET's Common Test Conditions (sequence classes, configurations AI/RA/LD) and the VVC Test Model reference software used to measure coding tools.
Quantization Parameter: controls how coarsely transform coefficients are quantised; higher QP means fewer bits and more distortion.
Sum of Squared Differences between two blocks; the ALF decision uses it to compare filtered and unfiltered blocks against the source.
Size, Weight and Power: the figure of merit for portable encoders alongside quality, latency and feature set.
A simulation harness that feeds a hardware module with stimuli and automatically compares its outputs with a software reference, bit for bit.
